notes.heading: Nucleophiles donate electron pairs
points: A nucleophile is electron-rich and has at least one lone pair, which it donates to an electron-deficient species (the electrophile).
Nucleophiles may be neutral or negatively charged: H2O, NH3, CH3NH2 (neutral); OH-, CN-, Cl-, Br-, I-, HS- (anions).
Donating the pair forms a new covalent (coordination) bond between nucleophile and electrophile.
A species with a full positive charge and no lone pair, such as (CH3)4N+, cannot be a nucleophile.

notes.heading: Nucleophilic substitution and leaving groups
points: The C-X bond in a halogenoalkane is polar, so carbon is delta+ and attacked by nucleophiles.
Nucleophile donates a pair to carbon while the C-X bonding pair moves onto X, which leaves.
Example: CH3CH2Cl + OH- → CH3CH2OH + Cl-. Nucleophile is OH-, leaving group is Cl-.
One bond forms and one breaks, so the nucleophile replaces the leaving group.

notes.heading: Heterolytic fission and curly arrows
points: Heterolytic fission is uneven bond breaking: one atom takes both bonding electrons and becomes an anion, the other becomes a cation.
A double-barbed curly arrow shows an electron pair moving; it starts at the bond and ends where the electrons go.
Breaking C-Br in bromomethane gives a methyl carbocation (CH3+) and a bromide ion, Br-.
These ions are unstable and short-lived, so they usually appear as intermediates.

notes.heading: Electrophiles accept electron pairs
points: An electrophile is electron-deficient and accepts a pair from a nucleophile to form a covalent bond.
Electrophiles are positive ions (such as CH3+) or neutral molecules with a delta+ atom (such as BF3).
Polar bonds from electronegative atoms create the delta+ site, e.g. carbonyl carbon in aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.
Non-polar Br2 can act as an electrophile once it is polarized by an approaching alkene.

notes.heading: Alkenes and electrophilic addition
points: The C=C bond is a region of high electron density, so alkenes are attacked by electrophiles.
This gives electrophilic addition: the reagent adds across the double bond.
Halogen X2 gives CnH2nX2; hydrogen halide HX gives CnH2n+1X; water (acid present) gives alcohol CnH2n+1OH.
Bromine water decolourizes (brown to colourless) with alkenes: a test for unsaturation.

notes.heading: Lewis acids and bases
points: Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor.
Lewis theory is broader than Brønsted–Lowry and covers reactions with no proton, such as BF3 + NH3.
In BF3 + NH3, NH3 donates a lone pair into boron's vacant orbital, giving F3B-NH3.
H+ is a Lewis acid; OH- and NH3 are both Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis bases.
AlCl3 can act as both a Lewis acid and a Lewis base (forms Al2Cl6 dimer).

notes.heading: Lewis acid-base reactions form coordination bonds
points: A Lewis base reacting with a Lewis acid forms a coordination bond, a covalent bond where one species supplies both electrons.
Nucleophiles are Lewis bases; electrophiles are Lewis acids.
A coordination bond can be drawn as a normal line or an arrow from the lone pair donor to the acceptor.

notes.heading: Ligands and complex ions
points: Transition element cations are Lewis acids; ligands are Lewis bases that donate lone pairs to them by coordination bonds.
A transition element ion bonded to several ligands is a complex ion, e.g. [Cu(H2O)6]2+.
Ligands include H2O, NH3, CN-, Cl-, OH-.
Overall charge = cation charge + (number of charged ligands × ligand charge).
Cation charge = overall charge − (number of charged ligands × ligand charge).

notes.heading: SN1 and SN2 in halogenoalkanes
points: Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2: one concerted step, a transition state, no intermediate, rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile].
In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, inverting the configuration; it is stereospecific.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1: slow loss of X- forms a carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks; rate = k[halogenoalkane].
Alkyl groups stabilize carbocations by positive inductive effect, so tertiary > secondary > primary; secondary can use either mechanism.
A transition state is a highest-energy, partly bonded arrangement; an intermediate is a more stable species in a multistep path.

notes.heading: Leaving group and rate of substitution
points: The rate-determining step involves heterolytic fission of C-X, so a weaker C-X bond means a faster reaction.
Bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): C-F 492, C-Cl 324, C-Br 285, C-I 228.
Rate order: iodoalkane > bromoalkane > chloroalkane > fluoroalkane (virtually inert).
Down group 17 the C-X bond weakens and halide ions become more stable, so I- leaves most easily.

notes.heading: Electrophilic addition mechanisms
points: Br2 with an alkene: Br2 is polarized by the C=C, the delta+ Br is attacked, splits heterolytically to Br-, giving a carbocation, then Br- attacks.
HX is already polar: delta+ H is attacked by C=C, giving a carbocation plus X-, which then bonds to C+.
Water addition: H+ attacks C=C giving a carbocation, H2O attacks C+, the oxonium ion loses H+. H+ is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst.
Curly arrows: from C=C to the electrophile; from the bond breaking to the leaving anion; from the anion to C+.

notes.heading: Carbocation stability and Markovnikov's rule
points: With an unsymmetrical alkene, HX can add two ways, via different carbocations.
Alkyl groups donate electron density, so a more substituted carbocation is more stable.
The H adds to the carbon with fewer alkyl groups, so the positive charge forms on the more substituted carbon.
Propene + HBr: secondary carbocation is more stable, so 2-bromopropane is the major product and 1-bromopropane the minor.

notes.heading: Electrophilic substitution in benzene
points: Benzene's stable aromatic ring resists addition, so it undergoes substitution with electrophiles.
Nitration uses conc. HNO3 with conc. H2SO4 (50 °C) to give the electrophile NO2+.
NO2+ is attracted to the delocalized pi electrons; the ring donates two electrons, forming a C-N bond and a carbocation intermediate.
Attack breaks aromaticity, which needs energy, so this is the rate-determining step.
Water removes H+ from the intermediate, restoring the aromatic ring and giving nitrobenzene.

definitions.definition: A reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons, from a lone pair; it may be neutral or negatively charged.
definitions.trap: Saying a nucleophile must be negative; neutral molecules like NH3 and H2O also count.

definitions.definition: A reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from it; it is positive or has a delta+ atom.
definitions.trap: Calling it merely 'attracted to electrons' without stating it accepts an electron pair.

definitions.definition: A reaction in which a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond while another bond breaks, releasing a leaving group.
definitions.trap: Vague answers omit that one bond forms as another breaks and a leaving group departs.

definitions.definition: Breaking of a covalent bond in which both bonding electrons go to one of the two fragments, forming a cation and an anion.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with homolytic fission, which gives radicals with one electron each.

definitions.definition: The atom or group that departs with the bonding electron pair when the bond to the electrophilic carbon breaks in substitution.
definitions.trap: Forgetting that the leaving group takes the bonding electrons with it as an anion.

definitions.definition: A reaction in which an electrophile attacks the electron-rich C=C bond of an alkene and adds across it.
definitions.trap: Mixing up with nucleophilic addition or substitution; alkenes are attacked by electrophiles.

definitions.definition: A species that accepts a pair of electrons from another species, forming a coordination bond.
definitions.trap: Giving the Brønsted–Lowry proton-donor definition instead; BF3 has no proton.

definitions.definition: A species that donates a pair of electrons to another species, forming a coordination bond.
definitions.trap: Giving only proton acceptor; Lewis base needs a lone pair to donate.

definitions.definition: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one species, a lone pair donated by a Lewis base to a Lewis acid.
definitions.trap: Treating it as a different bond type; it is a covalent bond.

definitions.definition: A Lewis base that donates a lone pair to a transition element cation, forming a coordination bond in a complex ion.
definitions.trap: Thinking ligands must be neutral; anions such as CN-, Cl-, OH- are ligands too.

definitions.definition: A transition element ion bonded by coordination bonds to several ligands.
definitions.trap: Forgetting overall charge is cation charge plus total ligand charges.

definitions.definition: An alkyl cation with the positive charge on a carbon atom, usually formed by heterolytic fission and short-lived.
definitions.trap: Thinking primary carbocations are most stable; tertiary is most stable.

definitions.definition: A one-step nucleophilic substitution, typical of primary halogenoalkanes, where the nucleophile and halogenoalkane both feature in the rate-determining step, via a transition state.
definitions.trap: Showing an intermediate; SN2 has only a transition state, and the product is inverted.

definitions.definition: A two-step nucleophilic substitution, typical of tertiary halogenoalkanes, where slow loss of the leaving group forms a carbocation intermediate; rate depends only on the halogenoalkane.
definitions.trap: Including the nucleophile concentration in the rate equation.

definitions.definition: In addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, hydrogen bonds to the carbon with fewer alkyl groups, so the major product forms via the more stable carbocation.
definitions.trap: Stating the rule without linking to carbocation stability (inductive effect) when asked to explain.
